newsitem.title: SWEDEN: UN's Annan calls for more aid for N. Korea famine.
newsitem.headline: UN's Annan calls for more aid for N. Korea famine.

text.p: United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan called on Monday for all countries to put aside their misgivings about North Korea to aid the victims of the communist nation's severe famine.
Annan said there was not as much international support for aid efforts in North Korea as he would like to see.
"There are certain military and political conditions that are making governments hold back," Annan told a news conference at the start of a four week Nordic trip.
"But I hope we will think of the children and the people."

Humanitarian aid groups are active in North Korea where an estimated 800,000 children are malnourished, but Annan said not enough was being done. At least 80,000 children are said to be severely malnourished and in danger of dying from starvation and disease.
UNICEF, which recently tripled its aid appeals to US$14.3 million, has described the situation in North Korea as worse than the famine in Ethiopia in the mid-1980s.
Two years of floods in North Korea had already depleted food stocks so when the country was hit by drought this year the situation became dire.

The United States, South Korea and Japan, among others, have at one time or another indirectly linked food aid to North Korea's presence at peace talks. North Korea, in turn, has set political conditions in exchange for its cooperation.
Annan said links to the peace process should be put to one side.
"I think the government is prepared to accept aid. They know they need food desperately," Annan said. "I think we should give them all the support we can without making conditions."
He said the UN could do a lot if it had the support of its member states.
"We are talking about the will and generosity of member states," Annan said. "Is the will there? Only time will tell."

U.S. officials remain optimistic about prospects for launching four-nation Korean peace talks but have ruled out negotiating North Korea's demand for a withdrawal of 37,000 American forces from South Korea.

The peace negotiations, proposed by Washington and Seoul last year, are aimed at replacing the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a more durable peace agreement for the bitterly divided Korean peninsula.

The four main combatants in the Korean War -- the U.S., South Korea and North Korea -- have agreed on Geneva as the site for formal talks to be held six weeks after a preparatory meeting in New York on September 15 but the agenda has yet to be agreed.
